final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

Email DogTraining@hssv.org. Also ask about their adopter price — they advertise a discounted/complimentary rate with proof of adoption, and your dog is a rescue.

**Short answers:**
1. **Hybrid, weighted toward DIY.** Leash pulling is pure mechanics and you can do it yourself. The barking is an emotional problem where a pro adds real value on exactly two points — telling you whether this is fear or frustration (they look identical on leash, the protocols differ), and setting your threshold distance. A ~$300 reactive-dog class buys both. A $2,400 private program mostly buys convenience.
2. **Three options with verified prices:** HSSV $300 (6 wks online, Wed evenings) · South Bay Dog Training in Campbell $360 (in-person Sundays + Tue 7pm Zoom, uses barriers — best format, but the 16 Aug round is FULL) · Orion in San Jose $395 (Sat 26 Sept 5:30pm, and a **free 20-min phone consult** worth taking regardless). D For Dogz at $2,400 is in the report as the premium fallback.
3. **Four-week plan** built as two tracks: loose-leash mechanics (front-clip harness, Be a Tree / Penalty Yards / 300 Peck) and Engage-Disengage for the barking, run at a distance where your dog notices but doesn't react.

**Two traps I'd have fallen into:**
- **Paws4Training** ranks high for South Bay "growly dog" searches at an appealing $250 — it's in **Seattle**. Verified the street address.
- **Off Leash K9 San Jose** publishes real prices but is e-collar-based. Wrong tool for a fear/frustration problem, and South Bay Dog Training bans e-collars from class outright.

**Set expectations now so you don't quit in week 3:** four weeks gets you noticeably better pulling and, on reactivity, your dog *glancing at you instead of erupting* at a distance that would have triggered it in week 1. Not a dog that can pass another dog on a narrow pavement — that's a 6–12 month arc, and progress won't be linear.

**Your move:** six subtasks queued, all with the contact details in them. Two are genuinely urgent — the HSSV email and buying the front-clip harness. The Week 1 subtask (measure threshold distance, start a reaction log) you can start tonight without spending anything; that log is also the single most useful thing to hand a trainer at a first session.

Setting this to `waiting` — my part is finished, everything left needs you (a decision, an email, a phone call, a purchase). Nothing is blocked on me.

report.markdown:
# Training plan: 14-month rescue border collie mix, South Bay CA

Three answers, in the order you asked. All prices verified on each provider's own site on 2026-08-06.

> **Time-sensitive:** the cheapest and best-fitting class starts **Wednesday 19 August at 6:15pm — 13 days away.** If you do only one thing from this report, do that enrolment.

---

## 1. Hire a trainer, or do it yourself?

**Both — but cheaply. Do the daily work yourself and buy one structured class (~$300). Do not book a generic obedience class.**

Your two problems are different in kind, and that's what drives the answer.

**Leash pulling is a mechanics problem.** Genuinely DIY-able. There is nothing a trainer does in week one that you can't do with a front-clip harness and clear instructions. Paying $2,400 to be taught "stop walking when the leash goes tight" is poor value.

**Barking at other dogs is an emotional problem** — and this is where owners working alone usually go wrong. Three things justify professional input:

- **Diagnosis.** Leash reactivity typically splits into fear (the dog can't flee because it's leashed, so it escalates) versus barrier frustration (a friendly dog enraged that the leash won't let it greet). From the leash end these look identical — barking, lunging. The protocols diverge. Guessing wrong costs you weeks.
- **Threshold distance.** Nearly all DIY attempts fail by working too close, which just rehearses the reaction. A pro sets this number for you in one session.
- **Structure.** A reactive-dog class gives you controlled trigger dogs at a controlled distance. That is genuinely hard to arrange on your own — you can't ask strangers to stand still 40 feet away.

### Why the balance tips toward mostly-DIY here

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Age 14 months | In your favour. Adolescent-onset and freshly practised, not a years-deep habit. Argues against an expensive long program. |
| Your availability | Fits DIY well. The work wants 10–15 min/day, not long blocks. Evenings are also the quietest streets. |
| Border collie | Responds to short sessions (5–10 min), clear criteria, consistent handling. Gets *worse* with repetitive drilling and over-arousal games. Suits daily owner-led micro-sessions better than one weekly hour of class drills. |
| No bite history | Keeps you in "class and self-directed work" territory rather than needing a veterinary behaviourist. |

### The group-class trap
A normal obedience class puts a reactive dog in a room full of trigger dogs at close range — i.e. over threshold for an hour, rehearsing exactly the behaviour you're trying to remove. Only book a class that is *purpose-built* for reactive dogs, with barriers and spacing. All three options below qualify. HSSV's general obedience classes explicitly warn off leash-reactive dogs, and their Loose-Leash Walking workshop excludes them too.

### What would change this advice
Escalate to a certified behaviour consultant (CDBC) or veterinary behaviourist if you see: air-snapping, teeth on skin, redirecting onto you or the leash, reacting to dogs 100+ ft away, or reacting to dogs through the windows at home. None of those are leash-skills problems.

---

## 2. Local options with real prices

### Recommended: HSSV "Top Dogs" — $300
**Humane Society Silicon Valley** · DogTraining@hssv.org

- **Level 1: $300**, six weeks, **online via Zoom**. First session 90 min, then 5 × 50 min.
- **Next start: Wed 19 Aug 2026, 6:15pm.** Evening — fits.
- Built specifically for "leash or barrier reactivity". Covers threshold work, impulse control, calm exits, emergency exits, coping skills. Positive reinforcement.
- **Level 2: $300**, six weeks, 50 min/week **in person**. Prereq: L1 or instructor approval.
- **Level 3: $300**, six weeks in person — activity/sport based, continuing counter-conditioning around other dogs.
- Eligibility: dogs that bark, lunge or worry but have **not caused injury**. Age is fine.
- ⚠️ **HSSV does not offer private training or consultation to the public.** Classes only; they refer out.
- 💡 **Ask about the adopter price** — HSSV advertises a special adopter rate and complimentary training with proof of adoption. Your dog is a rescue; this is worth an email.

**Why it wins:** cheapest, soonest, purpose-built. The online format is an underrated advantage — your dog learns the mechanics at home, calm and under threshold, before you ever test them near a real dog. Then Level 2 transfers it in person. $600 gets you twelve weeks of structured progression.

### Runner-up: South Bay Dog Training — $360
186 E Sunnyoaks Avenue, Suite C, Campbell, CA 95008 · southbaydog.training

- **Reactive Dog 1: $360.** Five weeks = 4 × 45-min in-person + 5 × 45-min weekly Zoom Q&A + daily support group.
- In-person Sunday mornings; Zoom Q&A Tuesdays 7pm. Both fit your availability.
- **Reactive Dog 2: $360**, same structure, Sundays 10:00am.
- Drop-in practice sessions **$75** for L1/L2 graduates (not offered this round).
- Runs **with barriers** in a controlled environment — the best format of the three for a reactive dog.
- Gear rules: flat collar, martingale or harness only. **No prong, choke or e-collars.** 6ft non-retractable leash. Proof of one DHPP.
- ⚠️ **The Sunday 16 Aug 11:00am round is FULL.** Ask about the waitlist / next round.
- ⚠️ No phone or email published — **web contact form only**. Centre is appointment-only; don't turn up.
- Minimum two participants to run; no make-up classes.

### Third: Orion Dog Training — $395
San Jose · oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog

- **"My dog is reactive, now what?" — $395**, six weeks.
- Small group: 4–5 teams in a 3,000 sq ft indoor space. Whole family welcome. Homework with video explanations.
- Dates: Fri 28 Aug 1pm (**daytime — won't fit**), **Sat 26 Sept 5:30pm (fits)**.
- ✅ **Free 20-minute phone consult** to check fit. Force-free; keeps a referral network of other force-free trainers.
- Also runs **Control Unleashed** — a curriculum built for over-aroused dogs, a strong fit for a collie.

**Take the free call regardless of which class you book.** It's the cheapest possible route to the fear-vs-frustration answer.

### Premium option: D For Dogz — $2,400
Serves San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Campbell, Los Gatos, Mountain View, Cupertino, Palo Alto and more.

- **Private Coaching: $2,400 / 6 weeks** — they coach, you train the dog.
- **Day Training: $4,200 / 6 weeks** — their trainer works the dog directly; you join key sessions.
- Includes a 90-min goal-setting session, priority trainer access between sessions, a complimentary group class, three months of post-training support. $420 saving for enrolling in the full program.
- Sessions run **at your home and on your actual walking routes** — the strongest argument for the price, since that's where the behaviour lives.

**Verdict:** 7–11× the class options. Hold it in reserve for if the class route stalls after two months.

### Price comparison

| Option | Format | Fits evenings/weekends | Price |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HSSV Top Dogs L1** | 6 wks online | Wed 6:15pm ✅ | **$300** |
| South Bay Dog Training RD1 | 5 wks, 4 in-person + 5 Zoom | Sun am + Tue 7pm ✅ | $360 |
| Orion Dog Training | 6 wks in-person, small group | Sat 5:30pm ✅ | $395 |
| D For Dogz private coaching | 6 wks, your neighbourhood | Flexible | $2,400 |

### Two to avoid
- **Paws4Training ("Growly Dog", $250)** — ranks well in South Bay searches but the business is at 319 NE 45th St, **Seattle WA**. Not local. Ignore if recommended to you.
- **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** — publishes real prices ($500 first lesson including an e-collar, then $100/session) but the program is built around e-collar work. Adding punishment to a dog that is already fearful or frustrated works against you. Note that South Bay Dog Training bans e-collars from class outright.

**Context worth knowing:** California does not license or regulate dog trainers — no state exam, no required education, no oversight. Certifications (CPDT-KA, CDBC, KPA-CTP, CBATI, Fear Free) are your only real quality signal. Bay Area benchmark is roughly $150–$275/hr for private work and $200–$400 for a 6-week group series, which puts all three recommended options at or below market.

---

## 3. The first four weeks

**Structure:** two separate 5–10 minute sessions a day, never combined, plus a changed walk policy. Short sessions are not a compromise here — for a collie, 5–10 minutes beats long drilling, and repetition-without-purpose actively backfires.

### The rule that matters most
**Stop rehearsing the reaction.** Every walk where your dog barks and lunges is a practice rep of barking and lunging. For weeks 1–2 you *avoid* triggers rather than train through them. This will feel like doing nothing. It is the highest-value part of the plan.

### Track A — Loose-leash walking
Gear: front-clip harness. Clipping at the chest turns the dog sideways as they pull, so pulling stops delivering forward progress.

1. **Be a Tree** — leash tight, you stop dead. Leash loose, mark and move off.
2. **Penalty Yards** — pulling toward something desirable makes you turn and walk away from it, so pulling moves the target *further* away.
3. **300 Peck** — build duration. Reward at 1 step of slack, then 2, then 3. If the dog breaks, drop back down.

Sequence: stationary indoors → 90° pivots → single steps with frequent direction changes → driveway → quiet street. In exciting environments reset to 2–3 steps per reward and upgrade the treats.

### Track B — Engage-Disengage (the reactivity protocol)
Find the distance where your dog **notices but does not react**. That's the threshold. Below-threshold is the whole game — a dog over threshold cannot learn.

- **Level 1:** dog looks at the other dog → mark → treat. You are rewarding *noticing*. A rep counts when the dog turns to you for the treat after the mark. Get 3–5 clean reps at one distance before advancing.
- **Level 2:** dog looks at the other dog; wait 3–5 seconds for it to look away on its own → mark the disengagement → treat. No look-away within 5 seconds? Back to Level 1. Won't take the treat? You're too close — add distance and restart.
- **Level 3:** dog self-disengages unprompted.

Treats must out-compete the trigger: chicken, cheese, hot dog. Not kibble. Watch for stiffening, hard staring, a closed mouth — add distance immediately. Teach an **emergency U-turn** as a separate cue so you always have an exit.

### Week by week

**Week 1 — Stop the bleeding, get a baseline**
Buy the gear. Measure the threshold distance and write the number down. Move walks to quiet times and routes (early morning, late evening, cul-de-sacs, industrial streets at weekends). Add long-line sniffing/decompression in open empty spaces to drain arousal with zero trigger exposure. Track A indoors only, 5 min/day. **Track B not yet** — just avoidance and observation. Log every reaction: distance, the other dog, recovery time, whether your dog would still eat.
*Move on when:* you have a threshold number and 2–3 walks with zero reactions.

**Week 2 — Loose leash outdoors, Engage-Disengage Level 1**
Track A moves to driveway then quiet street, 10 min/day. Be a Tree + Penalty Yards on every walk, no exceptions. Track B begins: one deliberate weekend session parked at threshold distance somewhere dogs pass predictably and far away — a park edge, a school field perimeter, a shopping centre kerb watched from your car. Level 1 only. 5–10 min, then leave.
*Move on when:* 3–5 clean Level 1 reps in a row, dog eating readily throughout.

**Week 3 — Level 2, then close the distance slightly**
Shift to Level 2 **at the same distance** you succeeded at. Never change level and distance in the same session. Once Level 2 is solid, reduce distance by a small increment. Two weekend sessions plus one weekday evening. Track A adds distraction: practise where there are people, cars and smells but **no dogs**.
*Move on when:* your dog reliably self-interrupts and looks back at you at the working distance.

**Week 4 — Combine and consolidate**
Now hold loose-leash mechanics *while* a dog is visible at threshold distance — that combination is what a real walk actually demands, and it's harder than either piece alone. Introduce the emergency U-turn under mild pressure. Deliberately practise a **moving** trigger rather than a stationary one. Reduce distance further only if week 3 was clean.

### What four weeks realistically buys you
Leash pulling noticeably better on quiet streets. On reactivity, the win is **your dog glancing at you instead of erupting, at a distance that would have set it off in week 1.**

It is *not* a dog that can pass another dog on a narrow pavement. That's months away.

Calibrate against this so progress doesn't feel like failure: small improvements typically appear within 2–4 weeks of consistent counter-conditioning, and the early win is exactly "notices another dog and glances at you". Meaningful behavioural change is a 6–12 month arc; full reliability across varied real-world settings takes longer still. **Improvement is not linear** — some days will feel like square one. That's normal, not failure.

### If you book a class
This plan is still the right first four weeks. HSSV Top Dogs L1 (from 19 Aug) covers threshold work and calm exits and overlays directly onto weeks 2–4. Don't run two conflicting protocols at once — where your instructor differs from this, follow your instructor.

---

## Recommended path

1. **Email DogTraining@hssv.org this week** — enrol in Top Dogs L1 before 19 Aug, and ask about the adopter price. ($300, possibly less)
2. **Request Orion's free 20-min call** — get the fear-vs-frustration read. ($0)
3. **Buy the gear this weekend.** (~$60–80)
4. **Start Week 1 immediately** — don't wait for the class to begin.
5. **Ask South Bay Dog Training about the waitlist** as your in-person follow-on after HSSV L1.

Total realistic spend: **under $400.** Revisit D For Dogz only if you're genuinely stuck in October.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
Question 1 of the brief. RESOLVED.

RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid — do the daily work yourself, but buy a small number of private sessions (roughly 2-4) with a certified trainer up front. Do NOT sign up for a generic group obedience class.

REASONING:
- The two problems are different in kind. Leash pulling is a mechanical/skills problem and is genuinely DIY-able; there is nothing a trainer does in week one that a competent owner can't do with clear instructions. Dog-directed barking is an emotional/arousal problem, and that is where owners usually go wrong on their own.
- The single highest-value thing a pro gives you here is a diagnosis: fear-based reactivity vs. frustrated-greeter reactivity. These look identical from the leash end (barking, lunging) but the protocols diverge. Sources note leash reactivity commonly comes down to restricted escape routes vs. barrier frustration — a friendly dog frustrated at not being able to greet. Guessing wrong means weeks of the wrong exercise.
- Trigger distance ("threshold") is the other thing a pro sets for you in one session. Nearly all DIY attempts fail by working too close, which rehearses the reaction.
- Age is in your favour and argues against a long expensive program. At 14 months this is adolescent-onset and freshly practised, not a years-deep habit.
- Breed factor: border collie arousal patterns respond to short sessions (5-10 min), clarity and consistent criteria, and get worse with repetition-without-purpose and over-arousal games. This suits owner-led daily micro-sessions better than a weekly hour of class drills.
- Availability fits DIY. Evenings and weekends is plenty — the work wants 10-15 min/day, not long blocks. Evenings are also the easier time to find quiet streets.
- Group class caveat: a normal obedience class puts a reactive dog inside a room of trigger dogs at close range, i.e. below threshold for an hour. Only useful if it is a purpose-built "reactive dog" / "growly dog" class with barriers and spacing.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS to full DIY: nothing much — if budget is tight, one single assessment session plus the week-by-week plan is a legitimate floor.
WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS to hire-more-heavily: if there is any air-snapping, teeth on skin, redirecting onto you/the leash, or reacting to dogs 100+ ft away or through windows at home. Those escalate to a CDBC/veterinary-behaviorist conversation, not a leash-skills conversation.

EXPECTATION SETTING (so progress doesn't feel like failure): small wins in ~2-4 weeks of consistent counter-conditioning — the early win is the dog noticing a dog and looking at you instead of erupting. Meaningful change is a several-month project; reliability in varied real-world settings takes longer. Improvement is not linear.

THE ONE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: stop rehearsing the reaction. Every walk where the dog barks and lunges is a practice rep of barking and lunging. For weeks 1-2 you actively avoid triggers rather than train through them. This feels like doing nothing; it is the highest-value part of the plan.

TRACK A — Loose-leash walking (mechanical, do this anywhere quiet)
- Gear: front-clip harness. Clipping at the chest turns the dog sideways as they pull so pulling stops delivering forward progress. 6ft fixed leash, no retractable. No prong/choke/e-collar.
- Method 1 "Be a Tree": leash goes tight, you stop dead. Leash goes loose, mark and move off. Pulling stops the walk; slack continues it.
- Method 2 "Penalty Yards": pulling toward something desirable makes you turn and walk the other way, so pulling moves the target further away.
- Method 3 "300 Peck": build duration — reward at 1 step of slack, then 2, then 3, and so on. If the dog breaks, drop back down. In exciting environments reset to 2-3 steps per reward and upgrade the treats.
- Sequencing: start stationary in the house/yard, add 90-degree pivots, then single steps and frequent direction changes, then the driveway, then the quiet street.

TRACK B — Engage-Disengage for the barking (this is the reactivity protocol)
- Find and hold a distance where the dog NOTICES the other dog but does not react. That distance is the threshold. Below-threshold is the whole game — dogs over threshold cannot learn.
- Level 1: dog looks at the other dog → you mark (click or a word) → treat. You are rewarding merely noticing. A rep counts as successful when the dog turns to you for the treat after the mark. Get 3-5 clean reps at one distance before advancing.
- Level 2: dog looks at the other dog, you wait 3-5 seconds for the dog to look away on its own → mark the moment it disengages → treat. If it does not look away within 5 seconds, go back to Level 1. If it will not take the treat or is reacting, you are too close — increase distance and restart.
- Level 3: the dog self-disengages without prompting.
- Treats must out-compete the trigger: chicken, cheese, hot dog. Not kibble. Moist/high-value.
- Early stiffening, hard staring or a closed mouth = warning signs. Add distance immediately.
- Also teach an emergency U-turn as a separate cue so you have an exit when a dog appears at close range.

WEEK 1 — Stop the bleeding + gear + baseline
Buy front-clip harness, treat pouch, high-value treats, clicker. Measure the threshold distance (note the number of feet). Switch walks to quiet times/routes — early morning, late evening, cul-de-sacs, industrial streets at weekends. Add sniffing/decompression time on a long line in an open empty space to drain arousal without any trigger exposure. Track A indoors only, 5 min/day. Track B: NOT yet — just avoidance and observation. Log every reaction: distance, the other dog, your dog's recovery time.
Ready to move on when: you know the threshold number and have had 2-3 walks with zero reactions.

WEEK 2 — Loose leash outdoors + Engage-Disengage Level 1
Track A moves to driveway then quiet street, 10 min/day, Be a Tree + Penalty Yards on every single walk with no exceptions. Track B starts: one deliberate session at the weekend, parked at your threshold distance somewhere dogs pass predictably at a distance (a park edge, a school field perimeter, a shopping centre kerb from your car). Level 1 only. 5-10 min max, then leave.
Ready to move on when: 3-5 clean Level 1 reps in a row and the dog eats readily throughout.

WEEK 3 — Engage-Disengage Level 2 + close the distance slightly
Track B: shift to Level 2 at the SAME distance you succeeded at, do not move closer and change level at the same time. Once Level 2 is solid, reduce distance by a small increment. Two weekend sessions, one weekday evening session. Track A: add distraction — practise loose leash where there are people, cars and smells but no dogs.
Ready to move on when: dog reliably self-interrupts and looks back at you at the working distance.

WEEK 4 — Combine, then consolidate
Now put the two together: hold loose-leash mechanics WHILE a dog is visible at threshold distance, which is what a real walk actually demands. Introduce the emergency U-turn under mild pressure. Deliberately practise a moving trigger (a dog walking past) rather than a stationary one. Reduce distance further only if week 3 was clean.
End-of-4-weeks realistic outcome: leash pulling noticeably better on quiet streets; the reactivity win is the dog glancing at you instead of erupting, at a distance that would have set it off in week 1. NOT a dog that can pass another dog on a narrow pavement. That is a months-away goal.

CALIBRATION: expect small improvements in 2-4 weeks of consistent counter-conditioning; the early win is exactly "notices another dog and glances at you". Meaningful behavioural change is a 6-12 month arc and full reliability in varied real-world settings takes longer. Improvement is NOT linear — some days will feel like square one, and that is normal, not failure.

IF A CLASS IS BOOKED: this plan is still the right first four weeks. HSSV Top Dogs L1 (starts 08/19) covers threshold work and calm exits and will overlay directly onto weeks 2-4. Don't run a conflicting second protocol at the same time — follow the instructor where they differ.

subtasks.title: Decide budget ceiling and pick the trainer route
subtasks.description:
The only decision left. Options, all verified 2026-08-06:
- HSSV Top Dogs Level 1 — $300, 6 wks online, starts Wed 08/19/26 6:15pm. Recommended.
- South Bay Dog Training, Campbell — $360, 5 wks, in-person Sunday mornings + Tuesday 7pm Zoom. Aug 16 round FULL.
- Orion Dog Training, San Jose — $395, 6 wks, Sat Sept 26 5:30pm.
- D For Dogz — $2,400 private coaching over 6 wks, on your own walking routes.
Recommendation is the hybrid: HSSV L1 at $300 plus the 4-week plan you run yourself. Total outlay under $400 including gear. Only escalate to D For Dogz if you're still stuck after two months.
Just pick a number you're willing to spend and which route, then the next subtasks unblock.

subtasks.title: Email HSSV to enrol in Top Dogs Level 1 before Aug 19
subtasks.description:
TIME-SENSITIVE — the next Top Dogs Level 1 cohort starts Wednesday 08/19/2026 at 6:15pm, which is 13 days from 2026-08-06. If it fills or you miss it, the next start date is unknown.

Email: DogTraining@hssv.org
Page: https://www.hssv.org/behavior-management-classes/
Class: Top Dogs Level 1 (Online Only), $300, six weeks via Zoom. First session 90 min, then 5 x 50 min.

Things to include or ask in the email:
1. Confirm a spot for a 14-month border collie mix, barking/lunging at dogs on leash, no bite history.
2. ASK ABOUT THE ADOPTER PRICE. HSSV advertises a special adopter price and complimentary training for adopters — send proof of adoption if the dog came from HSSV. Could reduce or zero the $300.
3. Confirm whether Level 2 (in person, $300) runs straight after Level 1 so you can plan the sequence.

Note: HSSV does NOT offer private training or consultation to the general public, so don't ask for a 1-on-1 — they'll refer you out instead.

subtasks.title: Ask South Bay Dog Training for the Reactive Dog 1 waitlist
subtasks.description:
Backup / better-format option. Reactive Dog 1 is $360 for 5 weeks: 4 x 45-min in-person classes + 5 x 45-min weekly Zoom Q&A (Tuesdays 7pm) + daily support group. In-person sessions are Sunday mornings. Held with barriers in a controlled environment, which is the right setup for a reactive dog.

THE CATCH: the Sunday Aug 16, 11:00AM round is marked FULL. You need to ask about the waitlist and the next round's dates.

Contact form only — no phone or email is published: https://www.southbaydog.training/contact
Location: 186 E Sunnyoaks Avenue, Suite C, Campbell, CA 95008. By appointment only, don't turn up to ask.

Also confirm: minimum two participants needed for a class to run, and there are no make-up classes if you miss one. Vaccination requirement is proof of one DHPP.

subtasks.title: Take Orion's free 20-minute phone consult
subtasks.description:
Worth doing regardless of which class you book, because it's free and it gets you a professional opinion on the one question that matters most: is this dog FEAR-reactive or a FRUSTRATED GREETER? The protocols differ and guessing wrong costs weeks.

Orion Dog Training, San Jose: https://www.oriondogtraining.com/reactivedog
Request the free 20-min phone consult by text or via their contact form.
Their class 'My dog is reactive, now what?' is $395 for six weeks, 4-5 teams in a 3,000 sq ft indoor space. Next suitable date is Sat Sept 26 @ 5:30pm (the Fri Aug 28 1pm slot won't fit your evenings/weekends). They also run a Control Unleashed class, which is a curriculum built for over-aroused dogs and a good fit for a collie.

Questions to ask on the call:
1. Fear vs frustration — what does the barking pattern suggest?
2. What starting threshold distance would you use for this dog?
3. Force-free confirmation, and what happens if my dog reacts in class?

subtasks.title: Buy the gear before the first session
subtasks.description:
All of it is needed for week 1 and every class option requires most of it. Buy before the weekend.

- FRONT-CLIP HARNESS (the important one). Clipping at the chest turns the dog sideways when they pull, so pulling stops producing forward progress. The Freedom harness is a commonly recommended model.
- 6 ft fixed leash. NOT retractable — banned in these classes and useless for this training.
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist. You cannot do this work digging in a pocket.
- High-value moist treats: chicken, cheese, or hot dog pieces cut small. Kibble will not out-compete the sight of another dog.
- Clicker, or pick a marker word and use it consistently.
- Long line (15-30 ft) for decompression sniffing sessions in open empty spaces.

DO NOT BUY: prong collar, choke chain, or e-collar. South Bay Dog Training bans all three from class, and they work against a fear- or frustration-based problem by adding punishment to a situation the dog already finds stressful.

subtasks.title: Week 1: measure the threshold distance and start a reaction log
subtasks.description:
This is the first actual training action and everything else depends on the number you get. Do it this week.

THRESHOLD = the distance at which your dog notices another dog but does NOT react. Find it by having the dog at a distance where dogs pass predictably and walking slowly closer until you see the first stiffening or hard stare — then back off. Write the number down in feet. Every exercise in weeks 2-4 is run at or beyond this distance.

START THE LOG. For each reaction record: distance, what the other dog was doing (moving/still, big/small, barking back), how long your dog took to recover, and whether it would still take a treat. After a week this tells you and any trainer whether this is fear or frustration — the single most useful thing you can bring to a first session.

ALSO IN WEEK 1: switch walks to quiet times and routes (early morning, late evening, cul-de-sacs, industrial streets at weekends) so you stop rehearsing the reaction. Add long-line sniffing time in an open empty space to drain arousal. Loose-leash practice stays indoors only, 5 min/day. Do NOT start the engage-disengage work yet.

Done when: you have a threshold number written down and 2-3 walks with zero reactions.
